items.text: An LLM predicts the next token, in a loop
It produces plausible text, not looked-up facts
Tokens drive cost, limits and speed; count them with the API
Everything must fit the context window; the app resends history

captions.text: Welcome to Module 2.
In Module 1 you built a solid Python foundation.
Now we meet the engine behind every agent in this course: the large language model.
Before writing a single API call, you need a clear mental model of what these
systems do, and just as importantly, what they don't do.
You will be able to explain next-token prediction in plain words.
Understand tokens, and why they decide your cost, your limits, and your speed.
Reason about the context window, and what fills it up.
And know which controls you actually have over generation, on current models.
Here is the core idea, simplified but accurate.
A language model takes the text so far as input.
During training it saw an enormous amount of text, and its weights encode patterns
of how text continues.
Its output is not a whole answer.
It is a probability for every possible next token.
These percentages are just an illustration.
One token is chosen and appended to the text, and the whole thing goes back in to
predict the next one.
A long answer is just this loop, run hundreds or thousands of times.
This explains a lot of behaviour.
The model produces plausible text, not looked-up facts.
It can be confidently wrong, which is often called hallucination, and its knowledge
stops at its training cut-off.
That's why agents give models tools and documents to check facts, which is exactly
what this course builds.
So what is a token?
It's a chunk of text, often a whole short word, a piece of a longer word, a space,
or a punctuation mark.
For example, agents call tools, full stop, might be split into four tokens.
This is an illustration.
The exact split depends on each model's tokenizer.
A rough rule of thumb for English is about four characters per token.
Code, unusual words, and many other languages use more tokens for the same text.
When you need an exact number, don't guess, and don't use another company's
tokenizer.
Ask the API: it has a token counting endpoint for the exact model you're using.
You'll use it in lesson five.
Tokens matter for three reasons.
First, cost.
You pay per input token and per output token, and output tokens usually cost several
times more.
Second, limits.
Every request has a maximum size, measured in tokens.
And third, speed.
Replies are generated one token at a time, so long answers take longer.
Streaming, in lesson four, makes that wait feel much shorter.
The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can consider in one
request, input and output together.
Everything you send goes in: the system prompt with your instructions, the whole
conversation so far, any documents or tool results, and the new message.
Current models have very large windows.
Claude Opus 5.5, the model we use in this course, accepts up to one million tokens.
The reply must fit too, and it has its own cap: up to one hundred and twenty-eight
thousand output tokens on this model.
A huge window does not mean you should fill it.
Every token you send is billed on every request, and focused context usually gives
better answers.
Managing what goes into the window is a core agent engineering skill.
One more crucial fact.
When you chat with an assistant, it seems to remember what you said earlier.
But the model itself has no memory between requests.
Your application sends the whole conversation every time.
The model's weights don't change while you chat.
If your code forgets to send the history, the conversation is gone.
You'll see this happen in lesson three.
You control generation with a few levers.
The system prompt sets the role, rules, and style.
Max tokens caps the length of the reply.
Effort controls how much reasoning the model does, from low to max.
Higher effort means better answers on hard problems, but more tokens.
And you choose the model itself: Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku, trading capability against
cost and speed.
You may have read about temperature and top p in older tutorials.
On current Claude models those sampling settings are no longer accepted.
You steer the model with instructions, effort, and the model you pick.
Quick check.
Your app sends a new request without the earlier messages.
What happens?
The model simply doesn't know.
It has no memory between requests.
It only sees what you send in that request.
A language model predicts the next token, over and over.
It produces plausible text, not looked-up facts, so important claims need checking.
Tokens drive cost, limits, and speed, and the API can count them exactly.
Everything must fit in the context window, and your app resends the history every
time.
Next lesson, you make your first real API call, and take the response apart piece by
piece.
